target: AG1's claim that a federal Election Day holiday would reliably give working people, especially low-income retail/service workers, paid time to vote
objection: Federal holidays generally do not require private employers to close or provide paid leave; because many low-income workers are in private retail and service jobs that can remain open, a holiday would not reliably create paid voting time for them.

target: AG1's assumption that a holiday would remove the scheduling barrier for those most affected
objection: If workers cannot get guaranteed time off or pay to vote, the work-time barrier can remain largely intact, especially for low-income workers whose employers are not required to give leave.

target: AG1's broader claim that a holiday is the best way to increase turnout
objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is not an effective turnout strategy compared with more direct access reforms such as state-guaranteed time off to vote or automatic voter registration.

target: AG2's objection that a holiday only helps if employers are required to grant time off
objection: A holiday can still reduce scheduling pressure and shift broader norms around non-working time even if some private employers do not close, so lack of universal paid leave does not mean the policy has no effect.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday alone leaves the key barrier intact
objection: Voting-access reforms are not mutually exclusive; a national holiday can be combined with state time-off-to-vote protections or automatic voter registration, so the existence of other needed reforms is not a reason to reject the holiday.

target: AG2's argument that school-based caregiving constraints are unaffected
objection: Because Election Day as a holiday would typically close schools or put them on reduced schedules, it would free many parents and guardians from school-based timing and childcare constraints that otherwise make voting difficult.

target: AG2's claim that lack of guaranteed paid leave means the scheduling barrier remains fully intact
objection: Election Day voting is still possible outside standard work shifts for many people, and early voting or absentee options may also exist; therefore paid leave is not the only way to clear the scheduling barrier.

target: AG1's claim that many voters have practical time outside work shifts to vote
objection: In the U.S., polling hours largely fall within standard weekday work periods, so for employed voters without flexibility there often is not practical time outside the work shift to vote.

target: AG1's assumption that a typical worker can fit voting around a work shift
objection: Many hourly and shift workers cannot readily rearrange their hours, so the voting window often does not include practical time outside work for them.

target: AG1's claim that a federal holiday would reliably supply the paid time or schedule flexibility workers need
objection: Federal holiday status governs government operations but does not require private employers to close or provide paid time off, so it does not reliably create the voting time most working adults need.

target: AG2's argument that the OECD precedent should not be taken as evidence a holiday works
objection: The fact that 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays shows that such scheduling is feasible in real-world employment settings and should not be dismissed as inherently ineffective.

target: AG2's claim that a federal holiday would not reduce scheduling conflicts
objection: A national holiday would typically make schools close and many workplaces operate on reduced schedules, which would remove a key scheduling barrier for many Americans.

target: AG1's claim that a national holiday would help low-income workers by freeing them from school-based constraints
objection: Some school buildings are used as polling places; if schools are closed for the holiday, those polling locations may become unavailable and reduce practical voting opportunities in affected areas.

target: AG1's assumption that school closures only help voters
objection: If local polling locations close or become unavailable, voters—especially low-income voters with limited transportation and less flexibility—may face greater burdens traveling to alternative sites or waiting in longer lines.

target: AG2's comparative-effectiveness argument that other reforms are better
objection: The fact that other reforms might be stronger does not justify rejecting a holiday, because policy should not be refused merely for not solving every barrier or for being less than maximally effective.

target: AG2's premise that the holiday leaves low-income workers without useful time to vote
objection: A holiday reduces work and school schedule conflicts for many people and therefore does improve practical voting opportunity, so the comparative-effectiveness objection is insufficient to oppose it.

target: AG2's claim that a civic holiday would not help low-income workers because employers might still deny leave
objection: Making Election Day a civic holiday lowers the social and institutional cost of taking time to vote and can make it easier for workers, especially low-income workers with less bargaining power, to obtain practical time off.

target: AG2's claim that the holiday cannot help because polling-place voting still exists and thus no voting options are removed
objection: A national holiday does not abolish Election Day voting; it preserves voting options while adding scheduling flexibility, so it cannot make low-income workers worse off by eliminating the ability to vote.

target: AG1's assumption that school closures and holiday status automatically help voters
objection: Because school buildings are often used as polling places, holiday-related closures can remove voting sites and thereby reduce practical Election Day voting opportunities for some people.

target: AG1's assumption that a holiday cannot remove voting options
objection: A holiday can indeed remove voting options for some voters if polling locations become unavailable, so the claim that it only adds access without taking anything away is not guaranteed.

target: AG2's claim that school closures and workplace reductions do not help low-income voters
objection: Reducing scheduling clashes is especially likely to help low-income workers because they typically have less schedule flexibility, so a holiday is particularly beneficial to those most constrained by time.

target: AG2's objection that OECD precedent does not prove effectiveness
objection: If many comparable democracies use elections on weekends or holidays, then a holiday is at least a plausible and credible voting-access measure rather than an inherently ineffective one.

target: AG1's claim that holiday status reduces the work-time overlap for retail/service workers
objection: In retail and service sectors, holiday staffing is driven by customer demand and operating hours, so holiday designation often does not substantially change the required shifts during the voting window.

target: AG1's assumption that a holiday reduces required work time for low-income workers
objection: Because many low-income workers are in private retail/service jobs with employer-set shifts and no guaranteed paid leave, a holiday may not reduce their required work hours enough to create usable voting time.

target: AG1's broader claim that any holiday-based scheduling change is enough for low-income workers
objection: A policy whose practical effect depends on employer discretion is less reliable for workers with the least flexibility, so state-enforced time-off rules are a more direct and dependable way to address the barrier.

target: AG2's reliability critique of federal holidays
objection: Even if a federal holiday does not legally require paid leave, it still typically causes schools and many workplaces to operate on reduced schedules, which likely reduces overlap between required work time and voting hours for many shift workers.

target: AG1's claim that school/work reductions are enough to solve the barrier for low-income workers
objection: In many retail and service workplaces, businesses often remain open and school closure is not universal, so a holiday would not reliably reduce scheduling conflicts for low-income shift workers.

target: AG2's claim that holiday status leaves work/school overlap unchanged for many low-income workers
objection: A holiday typically causes schools to close and many workplaces to run on reduced schedules, so it is likely to reduce the real-world overlap between obligations and voting time for many hourly workers.

target: AG2's argument that staffing needs in open workplaces remain unchanged on a holiday
objection: Holiday status commonly changes retail and service staffing patterns and operating hours, so many low-income workers would get more non-work time within the election window.

target: AG1's claim that holiday status changes staffing enough to create usable voting time
objection: Private employers are not required to close or grant paid time off on a federal holiday, and many low-income hourly workers still work daytime shifts on holidays, so the overlap with polling hours often remains unchanged.

target: AG1's assumption that reduced schedules at schools and workplaces will reliably help low-income workers
objection: Low-income workers still often have little flexibility and little bargaining power, so even if some schedules change, a holiday-based reform is less reliable than enforceable state time-off rules.

target: AG1's claim that reduced overlap creates reliable practical voting time for low-income shift workers
objection: Polling-place voting can require travel and waiting, and a holiday does not guarantee enough protected time to complete the whole process, so reduced overlap does not reliably translate into completed voting.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday is reliable for low-income workers despite lack of job-protected leave
objection: Because low-income workers may still lose wages or risk their schedules/jobs if they miss work, a holiday without enforceable paid or job-protected leave is not a reliable way to ensure they can vote.

target: AG2's claim that travel and waiting mean a holiday does not help
objection: A holiday usually gives workers a much larger block of free time rather than just a narrow gap, so many low-income shift workers would have enough time to travel, wait, and complete voting.

target: AG2's premise that holiday status leaves most relevant workplaces sufficiently scheduled for the barrier to persist
objection: For many hourly workers, a holiday reduces required work/school overlap enough that the travel-plus-waiting-plus-processing time needed to vote can fit within the expanded free window.

target: AG1's claim that holiday designation likely expands low-income workers' free window to most of the day
objection: Many private employers do not reduce shifts enough on a federal holiday, so low-income workers' day is often still largely occupied by daytime work and the free window does not expand to cover most of the day.

target: AG2's claim that lack of paid leave is fatal to the policy
objection: If a holiday reduces or eliminates required work or school hours during polling times, workers can vote during non-work time instead of needing employer-provided leave, so lack of paid leave does not eliminate the benefit.

target: AG1's claim that reduced overlap is enough for workers to finish voting
objection: Voting can take travel and waiting time, and state time-off laws can be drafted to guarantee enough time to complete the full process, whereas reduced overlap alone does not ensure completion for low-income workers.

target: AG1's assumption that holiday status gives workers enough secure time to finish voting
objection: Because a federal holiday does not create enforceable job-protected leave, low-income shift workers may still have to leave before finishing voting or avoid attempting to vote at all.

target: AG2's claim that a holiday-based approach is less reliable than state time-off rules
objection: A holiday can create a larger block of time off for many workers and directly address the scheduling barrier by reducing work/school conflict, making it a workable reform rather than merely a symbolic one.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday would expand most low-income workers' free window to most of the day
objection: For many low-income hourly workers, daytime shifts still overlap most of polling hours even on a holiday, so the free window often does not expand enough to make voting easy.

target: AG1's broader conclusion that a holiday will reliably improve access for low-income workers
objection: A reform should prioritize reliable, enforceable access for those most burdened by scheduling constraints; if a holiday does not reliably expand usable voting time, it is inferior to state-mandated time off and other direct access measures.

target: AG1's claim that a holiday gives enough usable time for polling-place voting
objection: Polling-place voting takes more than just arrival time; travel and line/waiting time can exceed the limited free window that many hourly workers still have, so the holiday may not give enough usable time to complete voting.

target: AG1's claim that reduced schedule overlap reliably lets workers vote during non-work time
objection: Even with reduced overlap, without job-protected leave workers may not be able to stay through the full voting process or may risk job consequences, so the reform is not reliably sufficient.
